title: Call It Colour Field. The Artist's Own Catalogue Calls It Pop Art. Nobody Who Studies Him Calls It Either.
standfirst: This 1990 canvas is filed here as Colour Field Painting. Jorge Martins's own online catalogue calls him a Pop artist instead. Neither label appears anywhere in the Portuguese criticism written about his fifty-year career — and the real reason an American label keeps attaching itself to his work turns out to be more interesting than a tagging error.

sections.heading: Two Databases, Two Labels, Neither One Portuguese
sections.body: This 1990 canvas arrives tagged, in the record behind this page, as Colour Field Painting — the mid-century American school built around Mark Rothko, Barnett Newman and Morris Louis, washes of pure colour meant to work on the nervous system rather than the eye. Go looking for a second opinion and you get a different American import entirely: [WikiArt's own artist page](https://www.wikiart.org/en/jorge-martins) for Jorge Martins lists his movement as Pop Art, a label that fits, at most, one decade of a career that runs past fifty years. Two automated catalogues, describing the same Portuguese painter, have reached for two different mid-century American schools — and neither term turns up anywhere in the Portuguese-language writing about him: not in [his Wikipedia entry's sourced account of his work](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Martins_%28pintor%29), not in the Gulbenkian Foundation's own notes on his career, not in the gallery text that quotes him directly on what he thinks he is doing.

sections.heading: A War in Angola Put Him on a Train to Paris for Thirteen Years
sections.body: Martins was born in Lisbon on 4 February 1940. He studied architecture and painting at the city's Escola Superior de Belas Artes from 1957, left without finishing the course, and had made his first group-show appearances by 1959. In 1961, as Portugal's war to hold Angola began and the prospects for a painting career at home looked thin, he left for Paris. It was exile rather than an ordinary move — [his own Wikipedia entry](https://pt.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jorge_Martins_%28pintor%29) puts it at thirteen years before he properly returned — but it was not a lonely one. Júlio Pomar, Lourdes Castro, René Bertholo and the married painters Árpád Szenes and Maria Helena Vieira da Silva were already working the same city, a small colony of Portuguese names that had settled there years before him.

sections.heading: He Named Barnett Newman as an Influence Himself
sections.body: The Colour Field label is not pulled from nowhere. In 1973 Martins visited the United States, and by 1975 he had taken a studio in New York for roughly eighteen months, intensifying what [the Gulbenkian Foundation's own account of his career](https://gulbenkian.pt/cam/artist/jorge-martins/) calls one of the most significant lines of research in his whole output: the representation of light and its manifestations. Asked to name his own reference points, [he listed](https://galeriafernandosantos.com/jorge-martins/) Klee, Vermeer, Piero della Francesca, Mondrian, Malevich, Duchamp — and, distinctly, Barnett Newman and Brice Marden, alongside what he called simply "uma certa pintura americana," a certain American painting, prized for its pursuit of simplicity. Newman stood with Rothko and Morris Louis among the painters the term Colour Field was coined to describe. So the American label was not invented by a cataloguer guessing from the colour alone — it is a thread the painter tied into his own work himself. It just is not the thread any Portuguese critic picked up when they came to write about him.

sections.heading: This Exact Phase Already Has a Name — Just Not That One
sections.body: What Portuguese criticism documents in detail is the phase of Martins's work this 1990 canvas sits inside. Through the 1980s, in an assessment reproduced on his Wikipedia entry, the critic João Pinharanda describes the painter autonomising the elements of colour, steering them through abstract reveries freed from text and from any direct figuration of light — what Pinharanda calls, in the original, "uma solução quase musical," an almost musical solution. The handling is ascetic rather than lush: thin luminous lines that stay a minority against a neutral canvas, with nothing left in the frame that the picture does not need. A red, square, unpeopled canvas dated 1990 sits squarely inside that run, a year before Martins moved on again into the spiralling, Copernicus-referencing De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium series he showed in 1991. An almost musical solution is not, on the face of it, how anyone describes Rothko — and it is exactly the kind of description a Portuguese critic reaches for instead of reaching for his name.

sections.heading: Nobody Has Written Down Anything About This Specific Canvas
sections.body: None of that research turns up this actual painting. [WikiArt's entry for Red Abstraction](https://www.wikiart.org/en/jorge-martins/red-abstraction-1990) gives a title, a year and one tag — "Rectangle" — and nothing else: no medium, no owner, no exhibition it has ever hung in. The image was added to the site on 21 May 2013, twenty-three years after the date it carries, credited to a single editor's account rather than a curator. Even its listed dimensions, 570 by 568 pixels, are the size of the photograph WikiArt is hosting, not the size of the painting — nobody has published the canvas's actual measurements anywhere. Set against a painter with catalogued work in the Centre Pompidou, the Gulbenkian's Centro de Arte Moderna, Serralves and the Museu Coleção Berardo, this one canvas is close to undocumented: a title and a date, and not much else anyone has thought to record.

sections.heading: The Work That Actually Reaches People Doesn't Hang in a Gallery
sections.body: The fuller record makes that gap stranger rather than better explained, because Martins's widest public reach runs through different objects entirely. In 1989 he made [forty-four drawings illustrating Fernando Pessoa's Mensagem](https://www.lehmanncontemporary.com/en/artist/jorge-martins/), shown at the Museu de Macau. In 1995 a tile piece of his, Ocean Piece, went into the Lisbon Metro; a related azulejo work toured American museums that decade as part of a survey of Portuguese tilework, and from there passed permanently into a Washington Metro station, where it is catalogued today as transit art rather than painting. Martins, born in 1940, is still working, and Portuguese papers were still interviewing him in 2022 about why he thinks painting has not died. The canvas behind this page carries none of that institutional memory. It carries a colour, a year, and two labels that do not agree with each other, or with him.
